Worked example: wages in the NLSW panel

Source: vignettes/articles/wages.Rmd
wages.Rmd

The National Longitudinal Survey of Young Women followed a cohort of women from 1968 on. Stata Press distributes an extract, so the code below runs as it stands in either language. We regress log wages on age, experience, tenure, where the respondent lives, race, education, marital status, union membership and hours worked. With nearly 19,000 observations, p-values come cheap, and this is exactly where a fixed level of .05 stops being informative.

The data and the model 

library(alphaN)
library(haven)

nls <- read_dta("https://www.stata-press.com/data/r19/nlswork.dta")
nls$race <- factor(nls$race, labels = c("white", "black", "other"))

f <- ln_wage ~ age + ttl_exp + tenure + not_smsa + south + c_city + race +
  collgrad + msp + nev_mar + union + hours
webuse nlswork, clear
global controls age ttl_exp tenure not_smsa south c_city i.race collgrad msp nev_mar union hours
(National Longitudinal Survey of Young Women, 14-24 years old in 1968)

A p-value of .003 that favors the null

We start with the conventional standard errors. JAB() and alphan jab report the Bayes factor of every coefficient.

m <- lm(f, data = nls)
n <- nobs(m)
n
#> [1] 18964
round(summary(m)$coefficients[-1, ], 4)
#>           Estimate Std. Error  t value Pr(>|t|)
#> age        -0.0112     0.0006 -17.5205   0.0000
#> ttl_exp     0.0346     0.0010  34.5677   0.0000
#> tenure      0.0157     0.0009  18.1270   0.0000
#> not_smsa   -0.1957     0.0069 -28.4180   0.0000
#> south      -0.1063     0.0060 -17.7771   0.0000
#> c_city      0.0057     0.0067   0.8517   0.3944
#> raceblack  -0.1148     0.0067 -17.0358   0.0000
#> raceother   0.0255     0.0260   0.9822   0.3260
#> collgrad    0.3343     0.0070  47.7897   0.0000
#> msp        -0.0216     0.0073  -2.9463   0.0032
#> nev_mar    -0.0659     0.0092  -7.1400   0.0000
#> union       0.1373     0.0066  20.7412   0.0000

signif(JAB(m), 3)

Look at msp, whether the respondent is married with the spouse present. Its p-value is .003, which would earn two stars in most tables. The Bayes factor is 0.56: the data are somewhat more likely under the null hypothesis than under the alternative. This is Lindley’s paradox in an ordinary regression. (Bayes factors too large to store are Inf in R and about 8e+307 in Stata.)

The level that would have prevented this follows from the sample size alone, so it can be set before the regression is run.

alphaN(n, BF = c(1, 3, 10))
#> [1] 0.0016980428 0.0005186127 0.0001435126
alphan `=e(N)', bf(1 3 10)
Significance level calibrated to a Bayes factor       method: JAB

           n |         BF       alpha
-------------+------------------------
      18,964 |          1   .00169804
      18,964 |          3  .000518613
      18,964 |         10  .000143513

For moderate evidence the coefficient has to clear a level of .00052, about 96 times stricter than .05.

Clustered standard errors

Each woman appears in several survey years, so observations are not independent. With cluster-robust standard errors the picture changes: msp is no longer significant even at .05, and its Bayes factor drops to 0.045.

library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

V <- vcovCL(m, cluster = ~ idcode)
tc <- coeftest(m, vcov. = V)[-1, "t value"]
signif(JABt(n, tc), 3)
#>       age   ttl_exp    tenure  not_smsa     south    c_city raceblack raceother 
#>  1.46e+21  3.08e+69  2.68e+18  3.66e+50  3.61e+18  8.20e-03  2.04e+17  7.95e-03 
#>  collgrad       msp   nev_mar     union     hours 
#> 2.42e+122  4.51e-02  1.22e+01  1.19e+29  9.89e-03
regress ln_wage $controls, vce(cluster idcode)
alphan jab

Wulff and Taylor (2024) recommend calibrating with the total number of observations, the conservative choice, and then checking whether a conclusion survives at the effective sample size, which deflates the total by the squared ratio of the classical to the cluster-robust standard error. Take nev_mar, never married.

se  <- sqrt(diag(vcov(m)))[["nev_mar"]]
rob <- sqrt(diag(V))[["nev_mar"]]
ne  <- n_effective(n, se, rob)
ne
#> [1] 5525.372

alphaN(ne, BF = 3)
#> [1] 0.001007174
JABt(ne, tc[["nev_mar"]])
#> [1] 22.6055
alphan n_effective, n(`=e(N)') se(`se_nev') se_robust(`=_se[nev_mar]')
local ne = r(n_effective)
alphan `ne', bf(3)
alphan jab nev_mar, n(`ne')
Effective sample size from cluster-robust standard errors

-------------+------------------------

n = 5,525.37202

The effective sample size is less than a third of the total. The calibrated level roughly doubles, and the Bayes factor rises to 22.6. The coefficient clears the bar under either sample size, so the conclusion does not hinge on the choice.

A joint test

Is race related to wages at all? The test has two restrictions, so q is 2, and p is the 12 parameters that remain in the model, the intercept included. For joint tests the targeted effect is on Cohen’s f scale, and sqrt(0.02) is what Cohen (1988) calls a small effect.

m0 <- update(m, . ~ . - race)
Fs <- anova(m0, m)$F[2]
Fs
#> [1] 146.7599

klauerBF(n, Fstat = Fs, q = 2, p = 12, de = sqrt(0.02))
#> [1] 4.440275e+60
alphaN(n, BF = 3, method = "ES", q = 2, p = 12, de = sqrt(0.02))
#> [1] 0.0003748979
test 2.race 3.race
alphan klauerbf, n(`=e(N)') fstat(`=r(F)') q(2) p(12) de(sqrt(.02))
alphan `=e(N)', bf(3) method(es) q(2) p(12) de(sqrt(.02))
 ( 1)  2.race = 0
 ( 2)  3.race = 0

       F(  2, 18950) =  146.76
            Prob > F =    0.0000

Klauer et al. (2025) Bayes factor                     method: ES
prior: de = .1414, nu = 3, r = .05774, q = 2, p = 12

How much does the method matter?

Here are all six calibrations at this sample size, for a target of 3. For the two Klauer calibrations we target a standardized effect of 0.2 and give p, the 13 other coefficients including the intercept.

c(sapply(c("JAB", "min", "robust", "balanced"),
         function(mm) alphaN(n, BF = 3, method = mm)),
  ES     = alphaN(n, BF = 3, method = "ES", de = 0.2, p = 13),
  moment = alphaN(n, BF = 3, method = "moment", de = 0.2, p = 13))
#>          JAB          min       robust     balanced           ES       moment 
#> 0.0005186127 0.0007527044 0.0076127859 0.0104883658 0.0011279310 0.0001079127
foreach m in jab min robust balanced {
    alphan `=e(N)', bf(3) method(`m')
}
alphan `=e(N)', bf(3) method(es) de(.2) p(13)
alphan `=e(N)', bf(3) method(moment) de(.2) p(13)

The levels span two orders of magnitude, from about .0001 under the moment prior to about .01 under the balanced prior, so the method is a substantive choice to be made and reported in advance. Choosing a calibration goes through the options.

Other models

Nothing here is specific to linear regression. JAB() accepts glm() fits and alphan jab runs after any Stata estimator that stores e(b), e(V) and e(N).

g <- glm(union ~ age + ttl_exp + tenure + not_smsa + south + c_city + race +
           collgrad + msp + nev_mar, data = nls, family = binomial)
signif(JAB(g), 3)
#>       age   ttl_exp    tenure  not_smsa     south    c_city raceblack raceother

#>  collgrad       msp   nev_mar

In this model nev_mar has a p-value of .002 and a Bayes factor of 1.08. It would pass a conventional test while the data do not distinguish the two hypotheses.

What the level costs

A lower level means less power, and at design time the two should be chosen together. The standardized effect d is what the t statistic divided by the square root of the sample size estimates.

alphaN_power(n, d = c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1), BF = 3)
#> [1] 0.2366270 0.9996793 1.0000000
alphaN_power(n, d = c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1), BF = 3, method = "balanced")
#> [1] 0.5771707 0.9999924 1.0000000
alphan power 18964, d(.02 .05 .1) bf(3)
alphan power 18964, d(.02 .05 .1) bf(3) method(balanced)
Power at the calibrated significance level            method: JAB

           n |          d          BF       alpha       power
-------------+------------------------------------------------
      18,964 |        .02           3  .000518613      0.2366
      18,964 |        .05           3  .000518613      0.9997
      18,964 |         .1           3  .000518613      1.0000

Power at the calibrated significance level            method: balanced

           n |          d          BF       alpha       power
-------------+------------------------------------------------
      18,964 |        .02           3    .0104884      0.5772
      18,964 |        .05           3    .0104884      1.0000
      18,964 |         .1           3    .0104884      1.0000

With this sample the JAB calibration detects effects of 0.05 almost with certainty and an effect of 0.02 only about a quarter of the time.

Reporting

The report records the settings and the decision rule, ready to attach to a preregistration.

alphaN_report(n, BF = 3, power_at = c(0.02, 0.05))
#> # alphaN settings report
#> 
#> Generated on 2026-11-09 with alphaN 0.3.0.
#> 
#> ## Inputs
#> 
#> - Sample size (n): 18,964
#> - Target Bayes factor: 3 (moderate evidence)
#> - Calibration method: JAB: Jeffreys' approximate Bayes factor
#>   (unit-information prior, b = 1/n)
#> 
#> ## Result
#> 
#> - Calibrated alpha level: 0.000519
#> - Decision rule: Reject H0 if the two-sided p-value of the coefficient
#>   is at or below 0.000519.
#> - Interpretation: a significant result then corresponds to a Bayes
#>   factor of at least 3 in favor of the alternative under this prior.
#> 
#> ## Power at the calibrated alpha
#> 
#> - Against a standardized effect of 0.02: 0.24
#> - Against a standardized effect of 0.05: 1.00
#> 
#> ## Please cite
#> 
#> - Wulff, J. N., & Taylor, L. (2024). How and why alpha should depend on
#>   sample size: A Bayesian-frequentist compromise for significance
#>   testing. Strategic Organization, 22(3), 550-581.
#>   doi:10.1177/14761270231214429
alphan report 18964, bf(3) powerat(.02 .05)

The mapping from p-values to Bayes factors at this sample size shows why a .05 threshold would mislead: the whole range of p-values just below .05 corresponds to Bayes factors well below 1.
